claim: Alzheimer's disease pathology is characterized by plaques of amyloid beta (Aβ) and neurofibrillary tangles of tau.
source: Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology is characterized by plaques of amyloid beta (Aβ) and neurofibrillary tangles of tau.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about AD pathology, supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Aβ aggregation is thought to occur at early stages of Alzheimer's disease.
source: Aβ aggregation is thought to occur at early stages of the disease, and ultimately gives way to the formation of tau tangles which track with cognitive decline in humans.
evidence: This is a widely accepted hypothesis in the field, referenced in the introduction.

claim: Tau tangles track with cognitive decline in humans.
source: Aβ aggregation is thought to occur at early stages of the disease, and ultimately gives way to the formation of tau tangles which track with cognitive decline in humans.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the manuscript regarding disease progression.

claim: The crystal structure of an Aβ core segment (residues 16-26 with D23N mutation) was determined by MicroED.
source: Here, we report the crystal structure of an Aβ core segment determined by MicroED and in it, note characteristics of both fibrillar and oligomeric structure.
evidence: The structure determination is described in the Results section with crystallographic data in Table 1.

claim: The Aβ16-26 D23N structure contains characteristics of both fibrillar and oligomeric structure.
source: Here, we report the crystal structure of an Aβ core segment determined by MicroED and in it, note characteristics of both fibrillar and oligomeric structure.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis comparing the determined structure to known fibril and oligomer features.

claim: Structure-based peptide inhibitors reduce Aβ aggregation.
source: Using this structure, we designed peptide-based inhibitors that reduce Aβ aggregation and toxicity of already-aggregated species.
evidence: This is supported by ThT assays and TEM data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Structure-based peptide inhibitors reduce toxicity of already-aggregated Aβ species.
source: Using this structure, we designed peptide-based inhibitors that reduce Aβ aggregation and toxicity of already-aggregated species.
evidence: This is demonstrated by MTT toxicity assays shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The designed inhibitors reduce the efficiency of Aβ-mediated tau aggregation.
source: Unexpectedly, we also found that these inhibitors reduce the efficiency of Aβ-mediated tau aggregation, and moreover reduce aggregation and self-seeding of tau fibrils.
evidence: This is supported by biosensor cell assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: The designed inhibitors reduce aggregation and self-seeding of tau fibrils.
source: Unexpectedly, we also found that these inhibitors reduce the efficiency of Aβ-mediated tau aggregation, and moreover reduce aggregation and self-seeding of tau fibrils.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ThT assays and biosensor cell experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Aβ and tau fibrils share a common epitope.
source: The ability of these inhibitors to interfere with both Aβ and tau seeds suggests these fibrils share a common epitope, and supports the hypothesis that cross-seeding is one mechanism by which amyloid is linked to tau aggregation and could promote cognitive decline.
evidence: This is inferred from the dual efficacy of the inhibitors against both proteins.

claim: Cross-seeding is one mechanism by which amyloid is linked to tau aggregation.
source: The ability of these inhibitors to interfere with both Aβ and tau seeds suggests these fibrils share a common epitope, and supports the hypothesis that cross-seeding is one mechanism by which amyloid is linked to tau aggregation and could promote cognitive decline.
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by the experimental data showing Aβ can seed tau aggregation.

claim: Alzheimer's disease is the most prevalent form of dementia.
source: Although Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most prevalent form of dementia, there are limited treatments to alleviate symptoms and none that halt its progression.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge.

claim: There are limited treatments to alleviate AD symptoms and none that halt its progression.
source: Although Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most prevalent form of dementia, there are limited treatments to alleviate symptoms and none that halt its progression.
evidence: This reflects the current state of AD therapeutics as of the manuscript's writing.

claim: Extracellular senile plaques of amyloid beta are histological features of AD.
source: Histological features of AD are extracellular senile plaques of amyloid beta (Aβ) and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles of tau (Glenner et al., 1984; Goedert et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Intracellular neurofibrillary tangles of tau are histological features of AD.
source: Histological features of AD are extracellular senile plaques of amyloid beta (Aβ) and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles of tau (Glenner et al., 1984; Goedert et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Tau aggregation correlates better to disease progression than Aβ aggregation.
source: While Aβ aggregation is thought to occur at the early stages of AD, tau aggregation correlates better to disease progression, with characteristic spreading along linked brain areas, and severity of symptoms correlating to the number of observed inclusions (Tanzi, 2012; Hardy and Selkoe, 2002; Manczak and Reddy, 2014; Seward et al., 2013; Brier et al., 2016; Schwarz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references.

claim: Tau pathology shows characteristic spreading along linked brain areas.
source: While Aβ aggregation is thought to occur at the early stages of AD, tau aggregation correlates better to disease progression, with characteristic spreading along linked brain areas, and severity of symptoms correlating to the number of observed inclusions (Tanzi, 2012; Hardy and Selkoe, 2002; Manczak and Reddy, 2014; Seward et al., 2013; Brier et al., 2016; Schwarz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Severity of AD symptoms correlates to the number of observed tau inclusions.
source: While Aβ aggregation is thought to occur at the early stages of AD, tau aggregation correlates better to disease progression, with characteristic spreading along linked brain areas, and severity of symptoms correlating to the number of observed inclusions (Tanzi, 2012; Hardy and Selkoe, 2002; Manczak and Reddy, 2014; Seward et al., 2013; Brier et al., 2016; Schwarz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Structural information about aggregated forms of Aβ and tau has not led to successful chemical interventions.
source: Structural information about the aggregated forms of Aβ and tau is accumulating, but to date this knowledge has not led to successful chemical interventions (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and reflects the state of the field.

claim: A link between Aβ and tau pathologies has been noted in transgenic mouse models.
source: A link between the appearance of Aβ and tau pathologies has been noted in transgenic mouse models generated by crossing or co-expressing mutant Aβ and mutant tau, but the mechanism is not yet understood at the molecular level (Oddo et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The molecular mechanism linking Aβ and tau pathologies is not yet understood.
source: A link between the appearance of Aβ and tau pathologies has been noted in transgenic mouse models generated by crossing or co-expressing mutant Aβ and mutant tau, but the mechanism is not yet understood at the molecular level (Oddo et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement reflects the knowledge gap the study aims to address.

claim: Injecting Aβ seeds can induce tau pathology at the injection site and in functionally connected brain areas.
source: By injecting Aβ seeds derived from synthetic peptide, transgenic mouse or AD patient tissue, tau pathology can be found both at the site of injection, and also in functionally connected brain areas (Bolmont et al., 2007; Götz et al., 2001; Morales et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Tau aggregation follows Aβ seeding in 3D neuronal stem cell cultures expressing early onset hereditary mutations.
source: Tau aggregation has also been reported to follow Aβ seeding in 3D neuronal stem cell cultures that express early onset hereditary mutations to drive overproduction and aggregation of Aβ (Choi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The molecular linkage of Aβ to tau remains unresolved.
source: In spite of these observations, the molecular linkage of Aβ to tau remains unresolved.
evidence: This statement identifies the research gap.

claim: One proposed hypothesis is that Aβ causes downstream cellular changes that trigger tau phosphorylation and eventual aggregation.
source: Proposed hypotheses include Aβ causing downstream cellular changes that trigger tau phosphorylation and eventual aggregation, and/or a direct interaction and seeding of tau by aggregated Aβ (Ittner and Götz, 2011; Stancu et al., 2014; Morales et al., 2013).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by cited references.

claim: One proposed hypothesis is that there is a direct interaction and seeding of tau by aggregated Aβ.
source: Proposed hypotheses include Aβ causing downstream cellular changes that trigger tau phosphorylation and eventual aggregation, and/or a direct interaction and seeding of tau by aggregated Aβ (Ittner and Götz, 2011; Stancu et al., 2014; Morales et al., 2013).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by cited references.

claim: Aβ may be cleaved from APP inside endosomes and then exported.
source: One possible model for intracellular aggregation could be that Aβ is cleaved from APP inside endosomes, and then exported (Rajendran et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a proposed model supported by a citation.

claim: Smaller diffusible Aβ oligomers are proposed to be the toxic species.
source: Another model proposes that smaller diffusible Aβ oligomers are the toxic species (Lesné et al., 2006; Lambert et al., 1998; Benilova et al., 2012)
evidence: This is a widely discussed hypothesis supported by cited references.

claim: Oligomers of Aβ isolated from AD serum are sufficient to induce tau aggregation.
source: indeed oligomers of Aβ isolated from AD serum are sufficient to induce tau aggregation (Jin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Aβ has been found to co-localize intra-neuronally with tau and at synaptic terminals.
source: Aβ has also been found co-localize intra-neuronally with tau as well as at synaptic terminals, with increased interactions correlating with disease progression (Manczak and Reddy, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Increased Aβ-tau interactions correlate with disease progression.
source: Aβ has also been found co-localize intra-neuronally with tau as well as at synaptic terminals, with increased interactions correlating with disease progression (Manczak and Reddy, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Soluble and insoluble complexes of Aβ bound to tau have been detected in AD tissue extracts.
source: Furthermore, soluble and insoluble complexes of Aβ bound to tau have been detected in AD tissue extracts (Manczak and Reddy, 2014; Guo et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Soluble complexes of Aβ and tau promote aggregation of tau in vitro.
source: In vitro, soluble complexes of Aβ and tau have been found to promote aggregation of tau (Guo et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Aβ fibrils can seed tau in vitro.
source: while another study found that Aβ fibrils can seed tau (Vasconcelos et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Cross-seeding of tau by Aβ promotes tangle formation in AD.
source: Taking the evidence together, we hypothesize that cross-seeding of tau by Aβ promotes tangle formation in AD, which could be prevented not only by inhibiting Aβ aggregation, but also by disrupting the binding site of Aβ with tau.
evidence: This is the authors' hypothesis based on cited evidence.

claim: The amyloid core KLVFFA of Aβ binds tau.
source: In Aβ, both the amyloid core KLVFFA, along with region spanning the carboxy terminal residues were found to bind tau (Guo et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The carboxy terminal region of Aβ binds tau.
source: In Aβ, both the amyloid core KLVFFA, along with region spanning the carboxy terminal residues were found to bind tau (Guo et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Peptides from regions of tau in exons 7 and 9 bind Aβ.
source: Conversely peptides from regions of tau in exons 7 and 9, well as aggregation prone sequences VQIINK and VQIVYK located at the beginning of repeat 2 (R2) and repeat 3 (R3) of the microtubule domain (K18), respectively, were found to bind Aβ (Guo et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Tau sequences VQIINK and VQIVYK bind Aβ.
source: Conversely peptides from regions of tau in exons 7 and 9, well as aggregation prone sequences VQIINK and VQIVYK located at the beginning of repeat 2 (R2) and repeat 3 (R3) of the microtubule domain (K18), respectively, were found to bind Aβ (Guo et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: A computational seeding model predicts that the amyloid core of Aβ can form intermolecular β-sheet interactions with VQIINK or VQIVYK.
source: A computational seeding model predicts that the amyloid core of Aβ can form intermolecular β-sheet interactions with VQIINK or VQIVYK (Miller et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The amyloid core segment is an important sequence for Aβ aggregation.
source: On this basis, we hypothesized that an inhibitor capable of targeting the amyloid core, which itself is an important sequence for Aβ aggregation (Tjernberg et al., 1999; Bernstein et al., 2005; Marshall et al., 2016), might block both Aβ aggregation and tau seeding by Aβ.
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: The amyloid core segment has been observed in multiple conformations in steric zipper structures.
source: However, this segment has been observed in multiple conformations in steric zipper structures (Colletier et al., 2011) and fiber models (Lührs et al., 2005; Colvin et al., 2016; Qiang et al., 2012; Huber et al., 2015; Wälti et al., 2016), impeding structure-based inhibitor design.
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: The Iowa early onset hereditary mutation in Aβ is D23N.
source: In an effort to characterize a toxic conformation of this sequence, we focused our efforts on determining the structure of the segment 16–26, containing the Iowa early onset hereditary mutation, D23N (Van Nostrand et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The designed inhibitors blocked aggregation of Aβ.
source: Based on this structure, we designed several inhibitors and found that they indeed blocked aggregation of Aβ, prevented cross-seeding of tau by Aβ, and surprisingly, also blocked tau homotypic seeding.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in the Results section.

claim: The designed inhibitors prevented cross-seeding of tau by Aβ.
source: Based on this structure, we designed several inhibitors and found that they indeed blocked aggregation of Aβ, prevented cross-seeding of tau by Aβ, and surprisingly, also blocked tau homotypic seeding.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in the Results section.

claim: The designed inhibitors blocked tau homotypic seeding.
source: Based on this structure, we designed several inhibitors and found that they indeed blocked aggregation of Aβ, prevented cross-seeding of tau by Aβ, and surprisingly, also blocked tau homotypic seeding.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in the Results section.

claim: The efficacy of the inhibitors against both Aβ and tau implies a similar binding interface on both proteins.
source: We suggest that the efficacy of these structure-based inhibitors against both proteins, but not other amyloid fibrils, implies there is a similar binding interface displayed on both Aβ and tau aggregates, supporting the cross-amyloid cascade hypothesis in AD.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing dual efficacy.

claim: The inhibitors do not affect other amyloid fibrils.
source: We suggest that the efficacy of these structure-based inhibitors against both proteins, but not other amyloid fibrils, implies there is a similar binding interface displayed on both Aβ and tau aggregates, supporting the cross-amyloid cascade hypothesis in AD.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with α-synuclein and hIAPP shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Crystals of Aβ16-26 D23N used for MicroED were only a few hundred nanometers thick.
source: With crystals only a few hundred nanometers thick, we used micro-electron diffraction (MicroED) to determine the structure of Aβ residues 16–26 containing the hereditary mutation D23N, (Figure 1A), KLVFFAENVGS.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental procedure.

claim: The Aβ16-26 D23N structure revealed pairs of anti-parallel β-sheets.
source: The structure revealed pairs of anti-parallel β-sheets each composed of ~4000 strands, stacked into a fibril that spans the entire length of the crystal.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Each β-sheet in the Aβ16-26 D23N structure is composed of ~4000 strands.
source: The structure revealed pairs of anti-parallel β-sheets each composed of ~4000 strands, stacked into a fibril that spans the entire length of the crystal.
evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure.

claim: Neighboring sheets in the Aβ16-26 D23N structure are oriented face to back, defining a Class seven steric zipper motif.
source: Neighboring sheets are oriented face to back (Figure 1B, Table 1) defining a Class seven steric zipper motif.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The three C-terminal residues of Aβ16-26 D23N adopt an extended, non-β conformation.
source: In addition, the three C-terminal residues adopt an extended, non-β conformation which stabilizes the packing between steric zippers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The sheet-sheet interface in Aβ16-26 D23N is strengthened by interdigitating side chains.
source: The sheet–sheet interface is strengthened by interdigitating side chains, Lys 16, Val18, Phe20, Glu22 from the face of one strand, and Leu17, Phe19, and the N-terminus from the back of the other.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The Aβ16-26 D23N zipper has a shape complementarity of 0.76.
source: The zipper has an extensive interface with a high shape complementarity of 0.76 and a total buried solvent accessible surface area of 258 Å2.
evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure.

claim: The Aβ16-26 D23N zipper has a total buried solvent accessible surface area of 258 Å2.
source: The zipper has an extensive interface with a high shape complementarity of 0.76 and a total buried solvent accessible surface area of 258 Å2.
evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure.

claim: The Aβ16-26 D23N structure is partly identical to the structure of Aβ16-21 (crystal form-I).
source: This structure is partly identical to that of a shorter peptide segment, Aβ16–21, KLVFFA (crystal form-I) (Colletier et al., 2011), which we used successfully as a search model for molecular replacement.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison and successful molecular replacement.

claim: Both Aβ16-26 D23N and Aβ16-21 have class seven symmetry.
source: Both the longer and shorter segments have class seven symmetry.
evidence: This is observed from structural analysis.

claim: Aβ16-26 D23N and Aβ16-21 differ in registry.
source: However, the two segments differ in registry.
evidence: This is observed from structural comparison.

claim: Aβ16-21 maintains an in-register hydrogen bonding pattern.
source: The shorter segment maintains an in-register hydrogen bonding pattern while the longer segment is out-of-register.
evidence: This is observed from structural analysis.

claim: Aβ16-26 D23N is out-of-register.
source: The shorter segment maintains an in-register hydrogen bonding pattern while the longer segment is out-of-register.
evidence: This is observed from structural analysis.

claim: The strands of Aβ16-26 D23N are tilted away from perpendicular to the fibril axis.
source: That is, the strands of Aβ16–26 are tilted away from perpendicular to the fibril axis—a departure from canonical cross-β architecture.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The elongated beta strand from residues 16-22 has been observed in full length in vitro fibrillar structure determined by cryoEM.
source: This elongated beta strand from residues 16–22 has also been observed in the full length in vitro fibrillar structure determined by cryoEM (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) (Gremer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with a cited structure shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The antiparallel architecture and lack of registration of Aβ16-26 D23N suggest this assembly has characteristics of an amyloid oligomer.
source: The antiparallel architecture and lack of registration of Aβ16–26 suggest this crystalline 'fibrillar'-like assembly has some characteristics of an amyloid oligomer.
evidence: This is inferred from structural features and comparison with known oligomer structures.

claim: Structural studies of amyloid oligomers most frequently reveal anti-parallel β sheet architecture.
source: Structural studies of amyloid oligomers most frequently reveal anti-parallel β sheet architecture (Tay et al., 2013; Laganowsky et al., 2012; Sarkar et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Fibril structures have revealed parallel β sheets.
source: whereas fibril structures have revealed parallel β sheets (Lührs et al., 2005; Colvin et al., 2016; Wälti et al., 2016; Krotee et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Some short segments of Aβ show antiparallel β sheets.
source: with the exception of some short segments of Aβ (Colletier et al., 2011) and in Aβ1-40 containing the early onset hereditary mutation D23N which leads to in-register anti-parallel fiber deposition in plaques (Qiang et al., 2012; Tycko et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Aβ1-40 containing D23N mutation leads to in-register anti-parallel fiber deposition in plaques.
source: with the exception of some short segments of Aβ (Colletier et al., 2011) and in Aβ1-40 containing the early onset hereditary mutation D23N which leads to in-register anti-parallel fiber deposition in plaques (Qiang et al., 2012; Tycko et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Out-of-register stacking of anti-parallel β strands has been proposed to be the defining trait of toxic oligomers.
source: The out-of-register stacking of anti-parallel β strands has been proposed to be the defining trait of toxic oligomers (Laganowsky et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: Aβ16-22 has been proposed to form oligomers in silico.
source: The segment Aβ16–22 has been proposed to be able to form such oligomers in silica (Sun et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The laboratory has developed a Rosetta-based design strategy using steric zipper structures to design capping peptide inhibitors.
source: Our laboratory has developed a Rosetta-based design strategy using steric zipper structures to design capping peptide inhibitors for a number of amyloid proteins implicated in disease (Sievers et al., 2011; Seidler et al., 2018; Saelices et al., 2015; Soragni et al., 2016; Krotee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited references to previous work.

claim: The structure was truncated to residues 16-22 for the search model.
source: We chose to truncate our structure to residues 16–22 for the search model, omitting the residues not in the β strand.
evidence: This is a methodological decision described in the text.

claim: Six distinct inhibitor candidates were chosen from the first round of design.
source: From our first round of design, we chose six distinct inhibitor candidates; those that were identified as good candidates but containing strong amino acid similarities to other top inhibitors were discarded.
evidence: This describes the design process.

claim: The initial pool of inhibitors contained four L-form peptides (L1-L4) and two D-peptides (D1 and D2).
source: Our initial pool of inhibitors contained four L-form peptides, 2 each of 6 and 8 amino acids length, termed L1-L4, and two D-peptides six amino acids long, termed D1 and D2.
evidence: This describes the initial inhibitor set.

claim: Inhibitor efficacy was assessed at a 10 molar excess by testing prevention of Aβ1-42 toxicity on Neuro-2a cells.
source: We assessed the efficacy of the inhibitors at a 10 molar excess by testing if they prevented Aβ1-42 toxicity on Neuro-2a (N2a) cells, a mouse neuroblastoma cell line, (Olmsted et al., 1970).
evidence: This describes the experimental method.

claim: Cytotoxicity was measured using MTT dye reduction.
source: We measured cytotoxicity using 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)−2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) dye reduction (Mosmann, 1983; Liu et al., 1997).
evidence: This describes the experimental method with citations.

claim: Inhibitor D1 with sequence (D)-LYIWVQ eliminated the toxic effect of Aβ1-42.
source: Our toxicity assay revealed one inhibitor, D1 with the sequence (D)-LYIWVQ, that was able to eliminate the toxic effect of Aβ1-42 (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MTT assay shown in Figure 2A.

claim: None of the inhibitors were toxic to N2a cells alone.
source: none of the inhibitors were toxic to N2a cells alone (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the molecular model, smaller hydrophobic residues of D1 mimic interactions with the fibril interface.
source: In our molecular model of the inhibitor, smaller hydrophobic residues of D1 mimic interactions with the fibril interface on one side of the peptide, which promotes recognition, (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is shown in the molecular model in Figure 2B.

claim: Large aromatic residues on the other side of D1 block possible further interactions.
source: while the other side of the peptide positions large aromatic residues between Aβ residues, blocking possible further interactions (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in the molecular model in Figure 2C.

claim: Six new inhibitor designs were selected and tested in the second round of design.
source: We selected and tested six new designs.
evidence: This describes the design process.

claim: Four second-generation inhibitors were eight amino acids long (D1a-D1d).
source: Of the six, four were eight amino acids long such that the inhibitor would extend over more of our crystal structure, which we called D1a-D1d.
evidence: This describes the inhibitor design.

claim: Two second-generation inhibitors (D1e and D1f) were six amino acids long with slight sequence perturbations from D1.
source: The additional two, termed D1e and D1f, were six amino acids long featuring slight sequence perturbations from D1 (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the inhibitor design.

claim: Inhibitors D1b and D1d were effective at reducing Aβ1-42 toxicity at both tenfold excess and equimolar ratio.
source: We identified two of the eight amino acid long inhibitors, D1b and D1d, that were also effective at reducing AB1-42 toxicity at both a tenfold excess and at an equimolar ratio (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: All tested inhibitors (D1, D1b, D1d) elicited a dose-dependent response with estimated IC50 of less than 1 μM.
source: We found that all inhibitors elicited a dose dependent response, with all having an estimated IC50 of less than 1 μM.
evidence: This is based on dose-response experiments shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The cognate negative peptide control LC (L-form of D1) did not reduce toxicity.
source: The cognate negative peptide control, LC, the L-form peptide of inhibitor D1, did not reduce toxicity (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E.

claim: All inhibitors reduce fibril formation in a dose-dependent manner.
source: We observe that all of our inhibitors reduce fibril formation in a dose dependent manner, while the negative control peptide, LC, does not (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown by ThT assays in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The longer inhibitors D1b and D1d appear effective at an equimolar ratio.
source: The longer inhibitors, D1b and D1d, appear effective at an equimolar ratio.
evidence: This is observed in ThT assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At higher concentrations, the inhibitors appear to self-assemble but remain effective at reducing Aβ1-42 toxicity.
source: However, when assayed at higher concentrations, the inhibitors appear to self-assemble, but remain effective at reducing Aβ1-42 toxicity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and Figure 2E.

claim: TEM analysis confirmed the reduced abundance of Aβ1-42 fibrils after 72 hr.
source: After 72 hr, samples were taken for negative-stain TEM analysis, which confirmed the reduced abundance of Aβ1–42 fibrils.
evidence: This is shown by TEM images in Figure 3B.

claim: D1b and D1d were more effective at reducing fibril formation than D1.
source: D1b and D1d were more effective at reducing fibril formation than D1, although all three inhibitors showed near equal efficiency in reducing toxicity.
evidence: This is observed by comparing ThT and TEM data in Figure 3.

claim: Fibrils were observed in the equimolar ratio sample of Aβ1-42 with D1, but not with D1b and D1d.
source: Fibrils were observed in the equimolar ratio sample of Aβ1-42 with D1, whereas the comparable samples with D1b and D1d did not contain fibrils.
evidence: This is shown by TEM images in Figure 3B.

claim: Inhibitors D1a and D1c were less effective at blocking fiber formation.
source: Inhibitors that were not efficient at preventing toxicity, such as D1a and D1c, were also less effective at blocking fiber formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: All inhibitors reduced the formation of Aβ1-42 assemblies recognized by conformational monoclonal antibodies.
source: We used conformational antibodies to probe samples of Aβ1-42 incubated with a 10-molar excess of inhibitor overnight at 37°C. Binding by oligomer specific conformational antibody A11 and A11-O9, a monoclonal variant of A11, was reduced by all of our inhibitors (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by dot blot assays in Figure 3C and supplementary figures.

claim: The inhibitors reduced the abundance of Aβ conformations recognized by antibodies mOC24, mOC64, mOC104, and mOC116.
source: Additionally, the inhibitors reduced the abundance of Aβ conformations recognized by antibodies mOC24, mOC64, mOC104, and mOC116.
evidence: This is shown by dot blot assays in Figure 3C.

claim: Antibodies mOC24, mOC64, mOC104, and mOC116 bind fibrillar plaques from patient-derived AD tissue and/or 3xTg-AD mouse tissue.
source: These antibodies bind fibrillar plaques from patient derived AD tissue and/or 3xTg-AD mouse tissue (Hatami et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Adding inhibitor to monomeric Aβ1-42 prior to incubation had a marked difference from adding inhibitor to pre-formed Aβ1-42 oligomers.
source: We found that adding the inhibitor to monomeric Aβ1-42 prior to incubation had a marked difference from adding inhibitor to pre-formed Aβ1-42 oligomers.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing experiments in Figure 2E and Figure 4A.

claim: When co-incubated with monomeric Aβ, D1 was as effective as D1b and D1d at reducing toxicity.
source: When co-incubated with monomeric Aβ, the shorter D1 inhibitor was as effective as D1b and D1d at reducing toxicity
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E.

claim: When added to pre-formed Aβ assemblies, only the longer inhibitors D1b and D1d were effective at reducing toxicity.
source: however, when added to pre-formed Aβ assemblies, only the longer inhibitors D1b and D1d were effective at reducing toxicity (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Both D1b and D1d could fully ameliorate toxicity of aggregates at 10 μM.
source: Both of the longer inhibitors could fully ameliorate toxicity of aggregates at 10 μM, but D1d is more potent, with effective reduction of toxicity to 1 μM.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: D1d is more potent than D1b at reducing toxicity of pre-formed aggregates, with effective reduction to 1 μM.
source: Both of the longer inhibitors could fully ameliorate toxicity of aggregates at 10 μM, but D1d is more potent, with effective reduction of toxicity to 1 μM.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: D1b differs from D1d only at amino acid positions 6 and 7.
source: D1b differs from D1d only at amino acid positions 6 and 7.
evidence: This is stated in the text and can be verified from Figure 2D.

claim: The difference in efficacy between D1b and D1d is suspected to be conferred from residue 6.
source: We suspect the difference in efficacy is conferred from residue 6, because both inhibitors contain positively charged residues at position 7, but at position 6 D1b contains a Gln while D1d has a much bulkier Trp.
evidence: This is inferred from sequence comparison and efficacy data.

claim: Peptide inhibitors can both prevent aggregation initiation and block toxicity of aggregated assemblies.
source: Our results indicate that while peptide inhibitors can both prevent aggregation initiation and block toxicity of aggregated assemblies, the latter appears to be more sensitive to slight perturbations in inhibitor composition.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental data comparing different inhibitors.

claim: Blocking toxicity of aggregated assemblies is more sensitive to slight perturbations in inhibitor composition than preventing aggregation initiation.
source: Our results indicate that while peptide inhibitors can both prevent aggregation initiation and block toxicity of aggregated assemblies, the latter appears to be more sensitive to slight perturbations in inhibitor composition.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the efficacy of different inhibitors.

claim: The inhibitors do not disaggregate Aβ fibers.
source: We next performed TEM to determine if our inhibitors could disaggregate fibers, or if the fibers are being capped, as our inhibitor design would predict. We aggregated 10 μM Aβ1-42 for 72 hr at 37°C under shaking conditions, then added inhibitors at 100 μM and incubated overnight. As the fibers are still present, we presume that our inhibitors are indeed capping or coating the fibers at toxicity inducing interfaces, thus preventing further seeding or toxic effects (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown by TEM images in Figure 4B.

claim: The inhibitors cap or coat the fibers at toxicity-inducing interfaces.
source: As the fibers are still present, we presume that our inhibitors are indeed capping or coating the fibers at toxicity inducing interfaces, thus preventing further seeding or toxic effects (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is inferred from TEM observations and the inhibitor design.

claim: Inhibitor D1d binds to Aβ1-42 fibrils with an apparent Kd of 52 μM.
source: We performed SPR to verify that our inhibitors bind to fibers. We find that the most potent inhibitor of aggregated assemblies, D1d, binds to Aβ1-42 fibrils with an apparent Kd of 52 μM (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is measured by SPR shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The true Kd of D1d binding to Aβ fibrils may be lower than 52 μM due to D1d self-interaction and polymorphic Aβ fibrils.
source: We used a one-inhibitor-to-one-protein substrate model to fit the data; however, the true Kd may be lower due to the complication of D1d self-interaction and polymorphic Aβ fibrils.
evidence: This is a caveat noted by the authors based on experimental considerations.

claim: Fibrils of Aβ1-42 and Aβ16-26 D23N seeded aggregation of tau K18+.
source: We tested seeding of the microtubule binding domain of tau, K18+ (244-380) in a ThT assay at 37°C under shaking conditions and found that fibrils of Aβ1-42 and Aβ16-26 D23N seeded aggregation, though not as efficiently as fibrils of K18 (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown by ThT assays in Figure 5A.

claim: Aβ fibrils seed tau less efficiently than K18 fibrils.
source: We tested seeding of the microtubule binding domain of tau, K18+ (244-380) in a ThT assay at 37°C under shaking conditions and found that fibrils of Aβ1-42 and Aβ16-26 D23N seeded aggregation, though not as efficiently as fibrils of K18 (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown by ThT assays in Figure 5A.

claim: Aβ seeding of tau was also observed on full length tau in the presence of heparin.
source: This seeding effect was also observed on full length tau in the presence of heparin (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: K18 was unable to seed Aβ.
source: Conversely, K18 was unable to seed Aβ (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Aβ was able to produce intracellular aggregates in tau-K18 biosensor cells significantly greater than vehicle alone.
source: We transfected biosensor cells with tau40 or Aβ fibrils (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) to a final concentration of 250 nM. We found that Aβ was able to produce intracellular aggregates significantly greater than the vehicle alone, but only at around 2.5% efficiency of tau40.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Aβ seeding of tau in biosensor cells occurs at around 2.5% efficiency of tau40.
source: We found that Aβ was able to produce intracellular aggregates significantly greater than the vehicle alone, but only at around 2.5% efficiency of tau40.
evidence: This is calculated from biosensor cell data in Figure 5B.

claim: Other amyloid protein fibrils and non-fibrillar Aβ are not seeding-competent in the tau biosensor system.
source: We found other amyloid protein fibrils and non-fibrillar Aβ are not seeding-competent in this system (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), indicating the biosensor cell assay can faithfully differentiate between fibrils of amyloid proteins, which differ in their underlying structures and sequences.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: All tested inhibitors were able to reduce Aβ-mediated tau seeding at 20 μM final concentration.
source: All of our inhibitors were able to reduce seeding at 20 μM final concentration, while D1b showed a reduction in seeding at a concentration as low as1 μM (Figure 5DE).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: D1b showed a reduction in Aβ-mediated tau seeding at a concentration as low as 1 μM.
source: All of our inhibitors were able to reduce seeding at 20 μM final concentration, while D1b showed a reduction in seeding at a concentration as low as1 μM (Figure 5DE).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: D1d was more effective than D1b at inhibiting Aβ toxicity.
source: While both D1b and D1d reduced Aβ aggregate toxicity on N2a cells, D1d was the more effective inhibitor of Aβ toxicity, whereas D1b is the more effective inhibitor at reducing tau seeding.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing data in Figures 4A and 5D.

claim: D1b is more effective than D1d at reducing tau seeding.
source: While both D1b and D1d reduced Aβ aggregate toxicity on N2a cells, D1d was the more effective inhibitor of Aβ toxicity, whereas D1b is the more effective inhibitor at reducing tau seeding.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing data in Figures 4A and 5D.

claim: Fibrils of Aβ1-42 K16A/V18A/E22A did not seed tau in biosensor cells.
source: We found that the fibrils of Aβ1-42 L17R/F19R were able to seed similarly to WT Aβ1-42, while no seeding was detected from Aβ1-42 K16A/V18A/E22A.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Fibrils of Aβ1-42 L17R/F19R were able to seed tau similarly to WT Aβ1-42.
source: We found that the fibrils of Aβ1-42 L17R/F19R were able to seed similarly to WT Aβ1-42, while no seeding was detected from Aβ1-42 K16A/V18A/E22A.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Seeding by Aβ1-42 L17R/F19R was inhibited by D1b.
source: Seeding by Aβ1-42 L17R/F19R was inhibited by D1b, suggesting that residues K16, V18 and E22 create the seeding interface which is targeted by inhibitor D1b.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Residues K16, V18 and E22 of Aβ create the seeding interface targeted by inhibitor D1b.
source: Seeding by Aβ1-42 L17R/F19R was inhibited by D1b, suggesting that residues K16, V18 and E22 create the seeding interface which is targeted by inhibitor D1b.
evidence: This is inferred from mutagenesis and inhibition data.

claim: All inhibitors (D1, D1b, D1d) function in a dose-dependent manner to prevent tau40 aggregation.
source: We performed a ThT assay on 10 μM tau40, at 37°C with shaking and 0.5 mg/mL heparin and found that all inhibitors function in a dose dependent manner similar to our results with Aβ monomer, while the control inhibitor LC does not reduce tau aggregation (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Control inhibitor LC does not reduce tau aggregation.
source: We performed a ThT assay on 10 μM tau40, at 37°C with shaking and 0.5 mg/mL heparin and found that all inhibitors function in a dose dependent manner similar to our results with Aβ monomer, while the control inhibitor LC does not reduce tau aggregation (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The peptide inhibitors are not able to block aggregation of hIAPP or alpha synuclein.
source: The peptide inhibitors are not able to block aggregation of the amyloid forming proteins hIAPP or alpha synuclein, indicating that these inhibitors are specific for Abeta and tau, and are not general amyloid inhibitors (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The inhibitors are specific for Aβ and tau, and are not general amyloid inhibitors.
source: The peptide inhibitors are not able to block aggregation of the amyloid forming proteins hIAPP or alpha synuclein, indicating that these inhibitors are specific for Abeta and tau, and are not general amyloid inhibitors (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is concluded from experiments with other amyloid proteins shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: D1b was the best inhibitor of tau40 fibril seeding, with an IC50 of 4.5 μM.
source: We found that similar to our Aβ-mediated tau biosensor seeding experiment, D1b was the best inhibitor, with an IC50 of 4.5 μM.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B and calculated from dose-response data.

claim: D1 was slightly effective at inhibiting tau40 fibril seeding.
source: D1 was slightly effective, while D1d showed seeding reduction only when increased to 75 μM (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: D1d showed seeding reduction only when increased to 75 μM.
source: D1 was slightly effective, while D1d showed seeding reduction only when increased to 75 μM (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: D1b was most effective at inhibiting seeding by fibrils of tau mutants that left intact interface A of VQIINK, the solvent accessible interface of VQIVYK, and 3R tau.
source: We found that D1b was most effective at inhibiting seeding by fibrils of mutants that left intact: interface A of VQIINK which is thought to involve aggregation at site I277 of tau, the solvent accessible interface of VQIVYK as well as 3R tau (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D.

claim: A tau40 mutant combining all mutations did not induce seeding in tau-K18 biosensor cells.
source: As a control, we tested seeding by a mutant of tau40 that combined all of the different mutations, and found this mutant did not induce any seeding in tau-K18 biosensor cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E), despite forming fibrils when incubated with heparin, indicating that at least one of the known interfaces is needed for seeding.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D.

claim: At least one of the known tau interfaces is needed for seeding.
source: As a control, we tested seeding by a mutant of tau40 that combined all of the different mutations, and found this mutant did not induce any seeding in tau-K18 biosensor cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E), despite forming fibrils when incubated with heparin, indicating that at least one of the known interfaces is needed for seeding.
evidence: This is inferred from the null mutant experiment.

claim: Control inhibitor LC has little to no effect on seeding from any tau construct.
source: Control inhibitor LC has little to no effect on seeding from any construct (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Both the VQIINK and VQIVYK aggregation segments of tau are inhibited by D1b.
source: Taken together, these data show that both the VQIINK and VQIVYK aggregation segments of tau are inhibited by D1b, and suggest that each may share common structural features with the Aβ core that could allow for cross-seeding of tau by Aβ.
evidence: This is concluded from the tau mutant experiments.

claim: VQIINK and VQIVYK may share common structural features with the Aβ core that could allow for cross-seeding.
source: Taken together, these data show that both the VQIINK and VQIVYK aggregation segments of tau are inhibited by D1b, and suggest that each may share common structural features with the Aβ core that could allow for cross-seeding of tau by Aβ.
evidence: This is inferred from the inhibitor efficacy and structural considerations.

claim: Treating brain-derived lysates with D1b significantly reduced seeding by all tested brain tissue samples.
source: We found that treating the brain-derived lysates with D1b significantly reduced seeding by all tested brain tissue samples (Figure 7).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7.

claim: PSP tauopathy tissue was responsive to treatment with each of the inhibitors, with D1b displaying the most pronounced inhibition.
source: Interestingly, the PSP tauopathy tissue was also responsive to treatment with each of the inhibitors, with D1b displaying the most pronounced inhibition.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7.

claim: D1b recognizes a common toxic epitope found in both Aβ and in a variety of tau polymorphs.
source: We surmise that D1b recognizes a common toxic epitope found in both Aβ, and in a variety of tau polymorphs.
evidence: This is inferred from the efficacy of D1b against both AD and PSP brain lysates.

claim: Overlaying the Aβ segment crystal structure with structures of tau R2 and R3 reveals a high degree of structural similarity.
source: We find that overlaying our Aβ segment crystal structure with structures of tau R2 and R3 reveals a high degree of structural similarity both in the backbone, and also apparently in the complementarity of sidechains from each to intrinsically interdigitate (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown by structural overlays in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Aβ overlays well with tau R2 and R3 regions in both parallel and anti-parallel orientations.
source: Interestingly, Aβ overlays well with these regions of tau in both parallel and anti-parallel orientations, suggesting that either fiber or smaller oligomers could be capable of cross seeding on the ends of fibrils.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3 and discussed in the text.

claim: The amyloid core of Aβ and the regions VQIINK and VQIVYK can form similar structures in AD that are biochemically capable of cross-seeding.
source: On this basis, we suggest that the amyloid core of Aβ and the regions VQIINK and VQIVYK can form similar structures in AD that are biochemically capable of cross-seeding.
evidence: This is concluded from structural overlays and experimental data.

claim: Inhibitor D1b is able to reduce seeding from brain homogenates.
source: Consistent with our finding that regions of Aβ and tau share structural similarities, we found that the Aβ inhibitor D1b is able to reduce seeding from brain homogenates, indicating that the inhibitor is recognizing a disease-related structural motif, while D1 and D1d are much less effective.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7.

claim: D1 and D1d are much less effective than D1b at reducing seeding from brain homogenates.
source: Consistent with our finding that regions of Aβ and tau share structural similarities, we found that the Aβ inhibitor D1b is able to reduce seeding from brain homogenates, indicating that the inhibitor is recognizing a disease-related structural motif, while D1 and D1d are much less effective.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7.

claim: Inhibitor D1b can recognize at least two unique core interfaces of tau.
source: However, our tau mutagenesis results suggest that inhibitor D1b can recognize at least two unique core interfaces, and thus could be able to act on multiple strains of tau fibers.
evidence: This is concluded from the tau mutant experiments.

claim: The effective dose to reduce toxicity of aggregated species is higher than to delay aggregation of monomeric species.
source: Similar to other peptide-based amyloid inhibitors, the effective dose to reduce toxicity of aggregated species is higher than to delay aggregation of monomeric species.
evidence: This is observed from comparing experiments in Figures 2E and 4A.

claim: Inhibitors to prevent an aggregation nucleus are more promiscuous than those that ameliorate toxicity by binding to a distinct structure.
source: It appears that inhibitors to prevent an aggregation nucleus are much more promiscuous than those that ameliorate toxicity by binding to a distinct structure.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential efficacy of inhibitors.

claim: A direct interaction between the Aβ core and the amyloid-prone regions of tau facilitates cross seeding.
source: In summary, our results suggest that a direct interaction between the Aβ core and the amyloid-prone regions of tau facilitates cross seeding.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all experimental data.

claim: The inhibitors designed for the Aβ core segment prevent cross seeding of tau.
source: Our inhibitors designed for the Aβ core segment prevent cross seeding of tau, as well as tau homotypic seeding.
evidence: This is demonstrated by biosensor cell experiments.

claim: It is necessary to control aggregation of both Aβ and tau in order to treat Alzheimer's disease.
source: The entwined nature of these two proteins in AD suggests it is necessary to control aggregation of both in order to treat the disease.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.
